core.timing_notes:
PRIMARY RECORDS (verified directly). ATCSCC Advisory 111, "National Ground Stop": signature 26/11/13 20:54, effective time 132054-140430, event time 13/2053-14/0400. Text: "DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY... ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED." Cancellation is ATCSCC Advisory 005 of Nov 14, signature 26/11/14 01:19 (8:19 p.m. EST): "THE FAA COMMAND CENTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP HAS BEEN CANCELLED."

INTERIM ADVISORIES (reported by Hangar Debrief, not opened directly). Advisory 117 at 2121Z cited a "nationwide comms failure". Advisory 120 at 2246Z cited a "communications failure".

ONSET. The FAA Q&A (Nov 15) says the problem began "at approximately 3:30 p.m. ET". Duffy said at the Nov 13 briefing: "at 3:36 p.m., we experienced instability". Bedford (Nov 14, Aviation Week) said the FAA could not assess the cause "over the course of about 45 minutes" and implemented the ground stop "around 3:45". BankInfoSecurity, citing The Air Current, reports a 3:44 p.m. ground stop for flights to eastern U.S. airports before the nationwide order at 3:54.

END. The FAA Q&A and Duffy both give 8:15 p.m. ET for the resumption of traffic. The Command Center cancellation advisory is timestamped 8:19 p.m. EST. Nextgov reported "around 9 p.m. EST", an outlier. The duration above (4.35 h) runs from 3:54 to 8:15 p.m. EST. Outlets describe it as "more than four hours" (FAA, CNN), "nearly five-hour" (Reuters) or "five hours" (Wired).

TIME OF DAY. The router work was done during the day, on a Friday. The FAA said it "will reevaluate when we do replacement/maintenance work." Duffy (Nov 14) said remote-site switchovers are done during the day and big facilities at night.

ROOT CAUSE STATUS. As of the latest sources (Nov 19-20), no root cause had been announced. Bedford said Duffy would announce findings, and Ars Technica reported that could come as soon as Fri Nov 20. No announcement was found as of Nov 21.
core.what_failed:
The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network failed. It is a contractor-owned (L3Harris), largely legacy TDM (time-division multiplexing) telecom backbone linking more than 4,000 FAA facilities. Data flooded the network "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds" and made the FAA's "legacy equipment" unstable. That disrupted air-ground radio communications and radar feeds, with instability at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, spreading to several TRACONs.

It was not a full outage: "Some frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable" (FAA Q&A).

The FAA's initial investigation pointed to two sources:
- a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris was installing a new Juniper Networks router (HPE-owned) as part of copper-to-fiber (TDM-to-IP) conversion work, replacing a roughly 25-year-old Cisco router;
- a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, whose router Duffy said had been replaced about three weeks earlier.

L3Harris blocked both sites and the network stabilized. The FAA disabled the router's "broadcasting function" on the originating routers and on more than 60 other Juniper routers, paused Juniper installations, and fell back on the older Cisco routers.

Duffy (Nov 17) said this was the 69th installation of the router and that the previous 68 worked. An FAA spokesperson told CNN investigators were trying to determine "why a network function that was supposed to be disabled became active" (CNN paraphrase). HPE said its "equipment was working as configured." Root cause is undetermined as of Nov 20.

core.trigger_change_description:
THE CHANGE. An L3Harris engineer installed and connected a new Juniper Networks (HPE) router at a remote FAA radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. It replaced a Cisco router that the FAA says was produced in 2001 and was supposed to have been replaced in 2006 (Reuters). The work was part of L3Harris's copper-to-fiber (TDM-to-IP) conversion on the FTI network. Officials called it routine sustainment work, driven by carriers discontinuing old copper lines. Bedford said it was not part of the $12.5B modernization program.

TIMELINE OF THE EL DORADO CHANGE (single source: CNN, Nov 18, citing one source). L3Harris notified the FAA on Nov 9 of planned router-replacement maintenance, "with work set to begin at 9 a.m. on Friday, November 13". By Friday afternoon "the new router was connected" and the contractor had left the site. Hours later the engineer was escorted back in to retrieve the router.

OVERSIGHT ACCOUNTS CONFLICT.
- CNN's sources and the PASS union say the FAA escort only let the contractor in. An FAA spokeswoman's statement said the escort "is not there while the technician is doing work."
- The Washington Post (Nov 17, one person close to the investigation) says an FAA official supervised, tested and signed off on the work.
- Bedford said the engineer "was monitored by an FAA technician."

THE SECOND SITE. Per Duffy (ABC Nov 15; Reuters Nov 16), the router at the Amarillo, Texas radar site, also implicated, had been replaced by L3Harris "about three weeks earlier", i.e. roughly late October 2026. This rests on Duffy alone.

THE BROADER ROLLOUT.
- Duffy: El Dorado was the 69th Juniper installation; the 68 prior installs had no problems.
- Duffy (Reuters Nov 17): the FAA spent a year testing the Juniper routers at its tech center.
- Senate Democrats, citing L3Harris: 3,648 routers are slated for conversion; about 400 are installed and 69 operational.

POLICY CONTEXT (CNN sources). A March 2025 FAA memo shifted contractor maintenance from "requests" to "notifications", noting "this work will proceed without FAA approval." FAA spokeswoman Walden denied that this reduced oversight.

EARLY ACCOUNTS. On the evening of Nov 13, anonymous sources were cited by CBS News (an update to the L3Harris-operated network caused a reboot and crash) and MS NOW (a federal official said a "software update" caused the stop). These accounts were unconfirmed by the FAA and were superseded by the official router-installation account.

MECHANISM. The specific router function at issue has not been officially named beyond "broadcasting function". A single anonymous source told CRN the broadcasting feature "should have been turned off because it was communicating with 20-year-old Cisco routers."
core.vulnerability_remediation_link:
No official source describes the El Dorado (or Amarillo) router replacement as a security fix, vulnerability remediation, or fix for an AI-found flaw. The FAA, DOT and L3Harris describe it as routine copper-to-fiber (TDM-to-IP) sustainment work, driven by carriers discontinuing obsolete copper lines and replacing 2001-era Cisco routers.

Statements that touch on patching:

(1) Mullin, Nov 13 White House briefing: "as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology... it was overwhelming the older system." A reporter then asked Duffy, "Are you saying that it was the FAA patching a system that caused this outage?" Duffy answered by describing the old TDM system being "overloaded with data". He neither confirmed nor described a security patch.
https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-briefing-markwayne-mullin-sean-duffy-faa-ground-stop-november-13-2026/

(2) White House release, Nov 18: "these are separate incidents caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems." It quotes DNI Clayton: "Lots of institutions, because these vulnerabilities have been identified, are patching..." and "As a result of SI and the ability to scan systems more quickly, the ability to identify vulnerabilities has increased." It also quotes Rubio: "the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA." The release is a general framing of the week's outages and does not specifically say the FAA router change was a vulnerability patch.
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/11/no-indication-of-a-cyberattack-dni-clayton-and-secretary-rubio-on-recent-tech-outages/

(3) Clayton testified Nov 18 that the outages were "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes." Per PolitiFact/PBS, he stopped "short of blaming artificial intelligence-driven cyberdefense upgrades for the outages."
https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-mullins-house-hearing-on-faa-ground-stop-outages-and-dirty-bombs

(4) The Washington Sun (Nov 17), citing three anonymous sources, reported that bank executives and the NSA told Congress the week's outages stemmed from fixes for AI-identified vulnerabilities. The same article states: "It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down."
https://www.washingtonsun.com/technology/bank-ceos-nsa-tell-congress-ai-driven-patches-behind-outages

(5) The FAA Q&A answers "Did your upgrades and modernization efforts cause this?" with "No, this is due to the legacy TDM system causing instabilities."

(6) Juniper published a critical Junos OS / Junos OS Evolved security bulletin on 2026-10-14. No source links the El Dorado router or its configuration to that bulletin.
core.ai_statements:
AI-SPECIFIC DENIALS.
- Duffy, Nov 13 briefing, on whether the FAA's new SMART AI program was involved: "But that SMART system isn't plugged in to STARS and ERAM. It's not -- this is completely disconnected and I love that some people have said this would be the root cause. By the way, if it was, I would tell you that, but this is not even plugged in... So, there was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today." (Roll Call transcript)
- Mullin, Nov 13: "We've seen zero evidence that this was -- that this was a cyberattack or an SI attack." (Roll Call)
- Air Space Intelligence, maker of SMART, statement Nov 13 (5:34 p.m.): "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." (The Hill)
- Bedford, Nov 14 presser: "zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was." (ABC; Aviation Week)
- FAA Q&A, Nov 15: "Q: Was this caused by SMART system? A: No. The two systems are not related. SMART is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system."
- Duffy, Nov 17: called the idea that the router issue was tied to AI tools "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. (CNBC)
- Bedford, Nov 17: speculation that AI was involved was unfounded. (Reuters paraphrase)

WEEK-WIDE "SI" STATEMENTS (not FAA-specific).
- Mullin, Fox News, around Nov 16-17, on the week's outages generally: a tech-industry person believes "that it's the SI, he said, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is... When they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself... And it causes a system to be overran that weren't designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today." (The Hill, Nov 17)
- DNI Clayton (White House release, Nov 18): "As a result of SI and the ability to scan systems more quickly, the ability to identify vulnerabilities has increased." On Nov 18 he testified that AI "is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape."
core.cyberattack_statements:
FAA AND DOT.
- FAA Q&A, Nov 15: "Based on all available evidence, we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor."
- Mullin, Nov 13: "so far what we've seen, there is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process." He also said: "There's no chatter. We haven't seen any footprints... It appears that this was mechanically driven; however, we're still looking, so we're not going to rule that out."
- Duffy, Nov 14: "We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all."
- Duffy, Nov 15 (ABC): "we have no indication that this was a hack" and officials "don't think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install at all."
- Duffy, Nov 17: "I've been told by our national security three letter agencies that we weren't hacked, but I think it's important that we have all precautions." He asked FBI Director Kash Patel to send FBI personnel to the L3Harris lab. The FBI said it was working with DOT, FAA and L3Harris but had not taken possession of any equipment (Reuters, via Fortune).
- Fortune (Nov 15) reported Duffy did not "totally rule out" a cyberattack at that point.

WHITE HOUSE AND INTELLIGENCE COMMUNITY, Nov 18.
- DNI Clayton: "This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state."
- Rubio: "The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago… We have zero evidence..."
- Clayton testimony: "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

core.scale:
- A nationwide ground stop of all departures at all U.S. airports, with inbound international flights handled case by case.
- Instability at 17 of 22 ARTCCs and several TRACONs.
- About 3,500 aircraft were airborne and landed safely (FAA).
- The FAA says operators canceled about 12,462 flights on Nov 13, including 9,082 by major airlines, and notes that not all were caused by the ground stop. Bedford cited about 12,000 flights not completed, including roughly 3,000 GA/private.
- More than 18,000 flights were disrupted or canceled in the following days and more than 1 million passengers affected (Reuters). The WSJ, cited by Ars, reported more than 20,000 cancellations over the weekend.
- Reuters called it the longest U.S. nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Ars called it the third-ever nationwide ground stop.
core.sector: Aviation / air traffic control (federal government); telecommunications backbone
other_notable: Locating the source was slow (single source, CBS via Yahoo): L3Harris took several hours to pinpoint it, and its Melbourne, FL network operations center could not immediately identify the originating IP address. BankInfoSecurity, citing a Yahoo live blog, reports Bedford said tracing took about 45 minutes, partly because maintenance is logged on paper. https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/l3harris-struggled-location-outage-during-183640636.html

Duffy (Nov 18, CBS via Yahoo) on L3Harris: "They didn't identify and isolate. That concerns me." Earlier, on Nov 14 (CNN): "We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job." Bedford (Nov 18, PBS/AP): "I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it."

Testing and forensics are under way at the L3Harris lab in Melbourne, Florida, with the FAA, HPE/Juniper, Cisco and the FBI. Duffy said they were able to "recreate what happened in El Dorado". https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/icymi-trumps-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-shares-update-nationwide-ground

Senate Commerce Democrats asked for an immediate halt to router installations and a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper. They wrote: "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed." (CNBC Nov 17)
Precedent: on Nov 19, 2009, a Harris technician's router misconfiguration during an earlier FTI fiber transition disrupted 129 facilities (DOT OIG, cited by Ars Technica and BankInfoSecurity).
Shares fell: L3Harris closed down 3.7% and HPE fell 4.5% on Nov 16 (Reuters).
The ground stop fell in a week of other outages: Microsoft 365 (Nov 12), JPMorgan Chase (Nov 16), the NSA network (Nov 17), Apple and United. Officials said these were unrelated to the FAA event.
Delta CEO Ed Bastian (Nov 16, Fortune) described the cause as "a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error."

Duffy is seeking $50 billion more from Congress for ATC modernization, including a new telecom network to replace the L3Harris-owned FTI: "Until I can build [the new architecture], I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network" (CNBC Nov 14).

PASS (the FAA technicians' union) said no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this upgrade, and that the technician's "orders were to simply let the contractor in the building" (CNN Nov 18).

core.what_failed: During validation of the weekly maintenance window for Disaster Recovery (DR) tenants, tenanted services in Workday's DR site "unexpectedly connected to Production databases." This left data "in an inconsistent state." Users could get errors accessing tenants, and jobs, integrations and tasks could fail with "missing transaction" errors. Workday put all WD1 production tenants into maintenance (Georgia Tech's relay also names WD5). During that time employees at affected customers could not log in, clock in or out, view pay, request time off or finish benefits enrollment, and scheduled jobs and integrations failed. To recover, Workday ran validation testing, then the weekly scheduled Service Update, then a re-index of its query service ("normally performed during our Quarterly Service Updates"), then released tenants in stages. A Workday spokesperson said the disruption affected two of the company's data centers.

Effective immediately, we are placing all WD1 Production tenants into Maintenance while our teams investigate the best recovery path. core.trigger_change_date: 2026-11-13. The validation of the weekly DR-tenant maintenance window happened that day; the exact time is not officially stated. Reddit posts relayed by UC Today, which UC Today did not verify, put the first DR-to-production connection at 8:50 a.m. PST (16:50 UTC).
core.trigger_change_description: Workday was validating the weekly maintenance window for its Disaster Recovery tenants. Its notice says the routine validation was the trigger. During that work, tenanted services in the DR site connected to production databases. No source says when any underlying configuration, credential, network route or code change that let DR services reach production was originally made. Workday has not published a technical root-cause analysis: DRJ, Security Boulevard, dev.to, CyberSec Guru, Kivorent and Nacionale reported none as of Nov 15–18, and none turned up in searches through Nov 21. CyberSec Guru notes that the event was separate from Workday's semiannual DR plan test. Iowa State University told staff on Nov 14 that Workday had "identified the root cause" and was doing final testing of a fix; this comes only from StatusStack's relay, and the cause was not described.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link: No source ties Workday's triggering change to a security fix, vulnerability remediation, or a fix for an AI-found flaw. Workday's stated trigger was validation of the weekly DR-tenant maintenance window. Related statements: Workday told the University of Chicago "this is not a security-related issue" (Nov 13), and a spokesperson said the outage was "not related to a cybersecurity incident" (WUSA9/ABC10, Nov 14). No explicit Workday denial of a patch or vulnerability-remediation link was found. A broader narrative tied the Nov 12–17 outage cluster to rushed patches for AI-found vulnerabilities. It came from The Washington Sun, Nov 17, citing three anonymous sources, and from the DNI's general remarks. The Cloud Security Alliance research note (Nov 18) found "no public evidence that such patching caused any specific outage in the cluster" and listed "Workday's DR test" among on-record causes that "do not fit" that claim. A Medium tracker (Nov 18) likewise noted that Workday's stated cause names no security work. HuffPost/Forbes (via Yahoo) wrote that the WSJ reported the root problem was "system upgrades gone wrong," citing several firms including Workday. That WSJ article is paywalled and its Workday detail was not verified.
core.ai_statements: No official Workday statement mentioning AI in connection with the incident was found. No source reports an AI system running the DR test. Sesame Disk commentary stated "There is no public evidence that an AI system ran the DR test." The AI denials made that week came from other organizations: the FAA said "zero evidence of anything AI related," and Microsoft said its outage was not related to "AI / agents." Neither applies to Workday.
core.cyberattack_statements: University of Chicago IT (Nov 13, 17:03 CST): "Workday has assured us this is not a security-related issue." Workday spokesperson (WUSA9, Nov 14): the widespread outage "was not related to a cybersecurity incident." The same statement was carried by ABC10 and WGRZ and quoted by UC Today. Several secondary outlets (CyberSec Guru, dev.to, Nacionale, MazeBolt) say the spokesperson told the Associated Press. No AP article about the Workday outage was found on apnews.com; the statement appears in TEGNA-station stories under a WASHINGTON dateline. The Cloud Security Alliance rated Workday's denial as a "Low" evidentiary gap because the mechanism was described. US officials said that week that there was no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack behind the outage cluster.
core.recent_security_patch_activity: No dated Workday security patch, emergency security patching or security maintenance in Oct 14–Nov 13, 2026 was found. Workday runs a weekly maintenance and Service Update window. WSU's schedule says Workday is unavailable each Friday 11 p.m.–3 a.m. Saturday Pacific (https://modernization.wsu.edu/workday-maintenance-schedule/). Georgia Tech described the vendor's regular Friday maintenance as beginning at 10 p.m. ET, and UChicago at 9 p.m. CST. StatusGator logged unacknowledged Workday unavailability in the early hours of Oct 10, 17, 24, 31 and Nov 7, 2026 (https://statusgator.com/services/workday); no source characterizes these as security work. In the same period, CISA urged immediate patching of critical PHP flaws (CVE-2026-109618/109619) on Oct 21, 2026 (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching). No source links Workday to that patching. On Oct 13, 2026 Workday announced it would acquire C1.ai, an agentic identity company; this was an acquisition, not a patch (https://security.workday.com/). The Java "Java4Shell" patch and CISA advisory came on Nov 17, after the outage.
vendors_or_suppliers_named: Workday (operator; no third-party vendor or supplier named in connection with the cause)
core.scale: Workday says it has more than 11,500 customer organizations. That is its customer base, not a confirmed count of affected customers; Workday said only "some of our customers," and WUSA9 reported it was not clear how many were affected. All WD1 production tenants were placed in maintenance, and WD5 production tenants are also named in a relayed notice. A Workday spokesperson said two data centers were affected. Downdetector logged nearly 3,000 reports shortly after 22:00 UTC (LiveNOW via UC Today). Georgia Tech relayed a Workday report that remediation was complete for "approximately 96% of all WD5 customers." Customers confirmed as affected include Emerson College, Washington University in St. Louis, University of Chicago, Georgia Tech, Florida Atlantic University, Iowa State, Saint Joseph's University, Calvin University, Smith College, Northeastern, Georgetown and others (StatusStack).
core.timing_notes: Start: Emerson College's status page says Workday took the system offline "at approximately 5:15pm E.T." on Nov 13 (22:15 UTC). UChicago says Workday informed it "around 4:15 p.m." CST (same instant). Engadget, via Kivorent, reported Downdetector complaints spiking about 5:19 p.m. ET. Unverified Reddit claims relayed by UC Today: first DR-to-production connection at 8:50 a.m. PT (16:50 UTC), internal escalation at 9:00 a.m. PT, first customer alert at 2:12 p.m. PT (22:12 UTC), and impact initially believed limited to WD5. The Workday cause notice was relayed at 01:00–01:05 UTC Nov 14 (FAU 8:00 PM EST; WashU 19:05 CST). Workday notice at 11:00 PM PST: validation succeeded and the weekly Service Update was beginning. Notice at 2:00 AM PST Nov 14: query-service re-index under way. FAU at 7:45 AM EST: majority expected by 11 AM EST. End: the Workday spokesperson said service was restored by 11 a.m. EST Saturday (16:00 UTC). Customer restorations ranged from Calvin at 9:45 AM EST (14:45 UTC) to Emerson at 10:27 AM EST, Georgia Tech at about 10:00 ET, UChicago Monitoring at 10:10 CST and Resolved at 13:35 CST (19:35 UTC), and WashU Monitoring at 11:24 CST and Resolved at 18:49 CST (00:49 UTC Nov 15). Saint Joseph's University's page showed maintenance from 00:59 to 16:54 UTC (15h55m). Duration of about 17.75 h is computed from 22:15Z to 16:00Z. Workday's Community maintenance page still showed "Workday is currently unavailable" at about 10:05 p.m. EST Nov 14 (StatusStack). Times of India mentioned further disruptions on Nov 14, "including a roughly one-hour incident"; this is single-source and unverified. Workday has no public status page. The incident began about nine hours before WSU's published production maintenance window (Fri 11 p.m. PT). Georgia Tech said it began "ahead of the regularly scheduled Friday maintenance period."
other_notable: Searches found no membership for Workday in Project Glasswing: it is not among the April 7 launch partners, and the roughly 150 organizations added June 2 are unnamed (https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing; https://www.anthropic.com/news/expanding-project-glasswing). None was found for OpenAI Daybreak / Trusted Access for Cyber either. The White House has not identified GOLD EAGLE participants (https://erp.today/gold-eagle-ai-vulnerability-coordination-erp-risk/), and searches for Workday with C2 ISAC returned nothing relevant.
No Workday post-incident report or technical RCA was found as of Nov 21, 2026. DRJ: 'Workday has not explained why its DR services were able to reach production.'

Workday's authoritative updates went through its login-gated Community status page; the public record comes mainly from university IT pages relaying vendor notices. Workday's X account had not posted as of Saturday morning (UC Today).
Emerson College extended open enrollment to noon ET Monday Nov 16. WashU gave out manual time-tracking forms and planned to rerun Autosys jobs.

Per CyberSec Guru, citing Workday's security datasheet and contracts: DR environment fully replicates production, RTO 12 hours, RPO 1 hour, DR plan tested at least every six months; standard SLA 99.7% monthly availability per UpperEdge (single secondary source).

Context only, with no source tying it to the outage: in September 2026 Workday said it would cut about 2.5% of its workforce (~500 roles), mainly in product and technology (SEC filing via Sesame Disk; Business Insider).
The outage was part of a Nov 12–17, 2026 cluster: Microsoft 365, the FAA ground stop, Chase, United, Apple and NSA Net. No official source links Workday's outage to the others.
Prior Workday outage referenced by Nacionale: November 2023 Portland, Oregon data center power failure.

core.org: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (Chase consumer and retail bank)
core.sector: Banking and financial services (retail and online banking, interbank payments, Zelle P2P)
core.start_utc: 2026-11-16, about 14:00 to 14:30 UTC (approximate). Downdetector reports began climbing "shortly after 9 a.m. ET" (Barron's via Yahoo Finance, cited by TechTimes). SpotOn's timeline puts it at "about 9:30 a.m." Eastern.
core.start_local: Monday 2026-11-16, about 09:00 to 09:30 EST (UTC-5). An NBC source said only that it "began Monday morning". A Washington, D.C. branch teller told Fox Business that in-store and online problems began "around 10 a.m." (single source).
core.end_utc: 2026-11-16, about 23:30 UTC. Around 6:30 p.m. EST a Chase spokesperson told NBC News: "Transactions are now posting normally." Al Jazeera converts this to 23:30 GMT.
core.what_failed: Chase transaction processing and posting were slowed or disrupted. This hit online and mobile banking (logins, balances, transfers and wires) and some in-branch transactions. Delays spread to any transaction with Chase as a party, including Zelle payments and transfers with Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Truist and others. The Chase app showed: "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later." Chase described the cause as "a software bug in on-premise hardware systems". An FBI official, cited by Fox Business, traced it to a software release Chase rolled out earlier that Monday that "affected a subset of its systems". Chase has not said which systems failed, how many customers were affected, or what went wrong in the software (TechTimes). An NBC source said: "This is really retail banking."
core.scale: Downdetector reports for Chase peaked at 4,822 shortly before 2 p.m. ET (Barron's via Yahoo, cited by TechTimes). Al Jazeera put the peak at "nearly 5,000". SpotOn, citing NBC, gave more than 4,600 at 1:50 p.m. Of Chase reports, 52% concerned balances and transactions, 21% web login and 17% transfers and wires (The Hill). Other banks shown on Downdetector: Bank of America (2,000+), U.S. Bank (1,000+), Wells Fargo (968), plus smaller spikes at Capital One, Citi, TD and Truist. Several of these banks said their own systems were unaffected. Chase has about 94 million U.S. customer relationships, 5,000 branches and 15,000 ATMs. NBC said it was "not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected." Chase handles an estimated 22% of Zelle transactions (Crone Consulting via American Banker, cited by TheStreet). JPM shares fell about 2.3% intraday (Barron's via Yahoo); no link to the outage was established.

Customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.

stated_cause_quotes.quote: Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. This is a technical issue, not cyber-related.

The agency told The Hill's sister network NewsNation that it didn't see any signs pointing toward malicious or external activity in the outage, finding that it was linked to a software release.

stated_cause_quotes.speaker: Chase spokesperson (to NBC News, around 6:30 p.m. ET)

The spokesperson said the problem traced back to "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems." The spokesperson added that the company did not identify that bug through AI tools or fix it with AI.

stated_cause_quotes.speaker: Jonathan Gould, Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), at an industry event on Tuesday, Nov 17 (Reuters; single wire)

stated_cause_quotes.speaker: Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence, House Homeland Security Committee (about the outage wave as a whole, including banks)

core.trigger_change_date: 2026-11-16. The FBI official cited by Fox Business said the software release was rolled out "earlier Monday" (single source for the timing). No source gives any earlier date for when the bug was introduced.
core.trigger_change_description: An unnamed FBI official told Fox Business that the disruption "was traced to a software release the bank rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems". The FBI separately told NewsNation (reported by The Hill) that the outage "was linked to a software release". JPMorgan's own wording names no release: "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems". No source says what the release contained, what it was for (feature, upgrade or security fix), or which hardware or vendor platform it ran on.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link:
Neither JPMorgan nor the FBI has described the Nov 16 software release as a security patch or vulnerability fix.

Chase-specific denials:
- A JPMorgan spokesperson told Fortune (Nov 18) that OpenAI's tools "were not a factor in the outage". The spokesperson also said the bank "did not identify that bug through AI tools or fix it with AI". This statement is about the bug; it does not address what the release was for.
- OCC head Jonathan Gould called it "an isolated incident" (Reuters).

Indirect or general ties, none naming Chase's release:
- A spokesperson for Sen. Mark Warner told Fortune that "botched implementation of those patches" (patches for AI-discovered vulnerabilities) was linked to the NSA outage and "the 'banking outages'". Single source.
- Washington Sun (Jeff Stein, Nov 17) cited three anonymous sources: "Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week's widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence". In the same article it notes that "banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs".
- Warner's Nov 17 public statement says the evidence "points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems" but does not name Chase.
- Reuters (Nov 18) cites experts linking outages generally to rapid patching, and an unnamed person said "at least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches". That bank is not identified.

Counterpoints:
- Times of India: "Not every failure this week fits neatly into the AI patching explanation", listing Chase among outages with "a different trigger".
- Fortune (Nov 17): "The FAA, Microsoft and Chase each gave their own explanation, and none blamed AI."
- American Banker quoted Bradley Leimer: "I'd be hesitant to connect it directly to Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, or others without more evidence."
core.ai_statements:
JPMorgan Chase spokesperson (Fortune, Nov 18; single source): OpenAI's tools "were not a factor in the outage". The company "did not identify that bug through AI tools or fix it with AI." Fortune notes that OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced a JPMorgan–OpenAI security partnership on Nov 5, a week and a half before the outage.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin (Fox News, Nov 16 night, about the outage wave including Chase): "I believe that it's the SI" ("super intelligence"), citing an unnamed tech contact. In the same interview he said "with 98% certainty, we're not seeing a cyber attack" and called the incidents "all individually unrelated" (Fortune, Nov 17). He later told CNBC: "they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system."

Sen. Mark Warner (statement, Nov 17, not Chase-specific): "What appears to be happening instead is a consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape..." A Warner spokesperson told Fortune that botched patch implementation was linked to the "banking outages".

Washington Sun (anonymous sources): bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches were behind the outages.

DNI Jay Clayton (Nov 18): the outages were "associated with maintenance and technical changes". He made no AI attribution.

Fortune (Nov 17): "none blamed AI" (the FAA, Microsoft and Chase).
core.cyberattack_statements:
Chase (X, Nov 16): "there is no evidence this is cyber-related." Evangelisti (AP): "it is not cyber-related." Earlier statement: "This is a technical issue, not cyber-related."

FBI official (Fox Business): "no indication of malicious or external cyber activity". The FBI told NewsNation it saw no signs of malicious or external activity (The Hill).

CNBC source (via Reuters): no indication bad actors were involved, and no sign one bug hit several banks at once (TechTimes).

Mullin: "98% certainty, we're not seeing a cyber attack." Clayton (Nov 18): "not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Warner: "no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort."

Reuters (Nov 18): the Treasury and the OCC called banks "minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident". The OCC plans a "deep dive" (anonymous source).

Separate incident: on Nov 19 Chase disclosed that third-party vendors were hit by a cyberattack that exposed some marketing data (customer names and email addresses). Chase said: "There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week." (https://x.com/chase/status/2123405210445857009)
programs_partnerships_memberships: Project Glasswing (Anthropic): JPMorganChase is a named launch partner, announced April 7, 2026, using Mythos Preview for defensive security work. Source: https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing. American Banker (May 21, 2026) says JPMorganChase is 'the only bank among Project Glasswing's named launch partners': https://www.americanbanker.com/news/anthropic-frees-mythos-partners-to-share-cyber-findings

OpenAI Trusted Access for Cyber: JPMorgan Chase appears in OpenAI's April 16, 2026 list of organizations that 'have already signed up to support these efforts'. Source: https://openai.com/index/accelerating-cyber-defense-ecosystem/

OpenAI Daybreak / strategic partnership: Greg Brockman disclosed the partnership at WSJ Tech on Nov 4, 2026 and posted on X on Nov 5. PYMNTS, citing the WSJ, says OpenAI will give JPMorganChase access to cybersecurity-focused models 'as part of the AI company's Daybreak program'. Sources: https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/openai-forms-jpmorgan-partnership-ahead-of-2027-ipo/ ; https://x.com/gdb/status/2118410818933203038 ; https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48718/jpmorgan-chase-signs-cybersecurity-and-coding-deal-with-openai

GOLD EAGLE (White House AI vulnerability clearinghouse, launched July 14, 2026): no source found naming JPMorgan as a participant, and the White House release names no companies. Politico (Sept 30, 2026) quotes JPMorgan cybersecurity executive director Benjamin Flatgard saying the Dimon-chaired Alliance for Critical Infrastructure will 'stand ready, ready and willing to help Gold Eagle and support that effort.' Sources: https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/07/white-house-launches-gold-eagle-initiative-for-unprecedented-cybersecurity-vulnerability-coordination/ ; https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/30/new-group-chaired-by-dimon-urges-private-sector-collaboration-on-ai-threats-01098366

Alliance for Critical Infrastructure (ACI): a CEO group chaired by JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, launched February 2026, to address AI-driven threats and shared vulnerabilities. Source: https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/30/new-group-chaired-by-dimon-urges-private-sector-collaboration-on-ai-threats-01098366

C2 ISAC: JPMorgan is not listed. The reported founding members are telecom carriers only (AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox, Lumen, T-Mobile, Verizon, Zayo). Sources: https://www.forbes.com/sites/ronschmelzer/2026/11/20/telecom-giants-are-preparing-for-a-new-era-of-ai-cyberattacks/ ; https://securityboulevard.com/2026/05/major-us-telecom-providers-form-c2-isac-to-coordinate-cyber-threat-sharing/
core.recent_security_patch_activity:
No source found documenting specific, dated security patches, emergency patching or security maintenance by JPMorgan Chase between about Oct 17 and Nov 16, 2026, other than the Nov 16 software release cited by the FBI official, whose purpose is not stated. No hardware or software vendor has been named, so vendor patch activity cannot be assessed.

Context only, none tied to JPMorgan by any source:
- PHP released an emergency fix for the AI-assisted 'PHP2Shell' flaws (CVE-2026-109618/109619) on Oct 21, 2026, and CISA issued a patch-immediately alert (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching).
- Reuters (Nov 18) said an unnamed "major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches" (https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/business/article318139753.html).
- Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said on Oct 14 that BofA added about 1,000 contractors to patch Mythos-found flaws (Fortune/CNBC). This is a different bank.
- JPMorgan published Michael Cembalest's 'Patchmageddon' paper on Jul 22, 2026, outside the 30-day window (https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/institutional/insights/market-insights/eye-on-the-market/patchmageddon/).
vendors_or_suppliers_named: Early Warning Services (Zelle network operator, co-owned by JPMorgan and other banks). Said Zelle was operating normally; not named as a cause.
OpenAI (security partner announced Nov 5, 2026). JPMorgan said OpenAI's tools were not a factor.
Anthropic (Project Glasswing / Mythos partner). Not linked to the outage by any source.
No hardware, platform or software vendor has been named for the 'on-premise hardware systems'.
core.timing_notes:
The outage fell on a Monday business day. Chase's cause statement on X was posted at 2026-11-16T20:57:08Z (3:57 p.m. EST), matching NBC's "around 4 p.m.".

Downdetector reports peaked around 2 p.m. EST (19:00 GMT) per AFP via Al Jazeera. TechTimes' figures: 4,822 shortly before 2 p.m., more than 3,400 at about 3:30 p.m., about 1,780 by about 4:45 p.m.

A D.C. branch teller told Fox Business the problems were resolved "just after 3 p.m." at that branch. Chase said "Transactions are now posting normally" at about 6:30 p.m. EST (23:30 UTC). Tom's Guide judged the outage over at about 7:40 p.m. (via SpotOn). Chase said on Tuesday, Nov 17, that services were back to normal (Business Insider).

Per the FBI official, the software release was rolled out "earlier Monday", the same day as the outage.

Surrounding events:
- 11 days after the OpenAI–JPMorgan security partnership announcement (Nov 4–5).
- 4 days after the Microsoft 365 outage (Nov 12) and 3 days after the FAA nationwide ground stop (Nov 13).
- Same day as a United Airlines system outage; one day before the NSA (NSANet) and Apple outages (Nov 17).
- Three days before Chase disclosed the vendor cyber incident (Nov 19).
other_notable: Regulators: Reuters (Nov 18) reported that the Treasury and the OCC called banks minutes after the incident was reported. Banks were asked to tell customers not to panic. The OCC plans a 'deep dive' to check that what it was told is correct (anonymous sources). An NBC source said regulators 'quickly determined this was contained'.
The Federal Reserve's systems, including interbank ACH, were operating normally per the Fed's website (ABC News via TechTimes).
Wells Fargo's website briefly showed a notice that some online banking features were not working; ABC said it was later removed. Wells Fargo declined to comment.

Statements from other institutions: Zelle said 'Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should.' U.S. Bank said its systems were 'not directly impacted'. Capital One, PNC and Truist said they were operating normally. Bank of America said its systems 'have been operating normally today.'
A JPMorgan Chase ATM in Irving, Texas was photographed out of service (AP via Yahoo). Branch computer systems were 'up and down' (Fox Business).
Banking Dive (Nov 20): Mayer Brown's Justin Herring said banks in Project Glasswing 'have been absolutely inundated with questions from their regulators' about patching-related outage risk.

Political follow-up: on Nov 19, Trump replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross with acting director Kirsten Davies after the outage wave (Fortune/AP). Senate Minority Leader Schumer asked for an intelligence red team to report by Dec 1.
Prior incident: Chase had a Zelle-related outage on July 25, 2023 (TechTimes, American Banker).

core.what_failed:

(2) ALPA's memo, seen by Reuters, described a "companywide web-based outage" hitting multiple pilot-facing applications, including crew communications and messaging.

(3) An internal company alert obtained by CNN (CNN only) said access was lost to multiple crew applications, including flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools. Pilots were told not to log out because they might not get back in. Pilots who could not reach flight plans were told to ask dispatchers to email them.

(4) At Chicago O'Hare, the pushback-request system went down. At Newark, the outage affected how ramp crews received gate changes (AirlineGeeks, from ATC audio).

(5) NBC Chicago, citing ATC audio, said aircraft could not receive "takeoff numbers" from dispatch.

United Express flights and flights already airborne were not affected. AP: United "had no further information to provide" on whether the Unimatic system, which failed in August 2025, was involved. core.scale:
NSANet, the NSA's classified internal network for sharing classified (including top-secret) information. Reporting describes it as essentially the agency's classified email system.
- The Fort Meade campus was closed to most employees ("code orange") from Tuesday night 11/17. The closure was extended on Thursday 11/19. Staff returned on staggered schedules on 11/20.
- A contractor told CNN the Fort Meade hub has "over 20,000 employees" and that some parking lots were "fully abandoned on Tuesday."
- CNN (four sources, single outlet) reported that the NSA cryptologic center in Georgia, which supports Middle East SIGINT and cyber operations, could not use NSANet to reach colleagues in the region and relied on workarounds.
- NSA said "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational."
- Five Eyes intelligence sharing was not affected, according to CNN sources.
- Reuters could not independently determine the extent or length of the outage.
- CNN called the length ("almost four days") "unusually long and disruptive."
core.what_failed:
NSANet, the NSA's classified internal communications network. Employees could not log in or had only intermittent service.
- The Record (single source) said the system was "not completely shut down, but was only providing intermittent service."
- Logins were staggered because "the login process is the most taxing process on the system."
- Per DNI Jay Clayton, systems being patched for the PHP vulnerabilities did "not come back up when you patch them as expected."
- NSA's own statement says only that it "experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and that "some internal systems were affected." It does not name the network or the cause.

core.trigger_change_description:
The NSA was applying software patches and updates for the critical "PHP2Shell" vulnerabilities in the PHP language (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, unauthenticated remote code execution). DNI Clayton said the patched systems did not come back up as expected.
- Corroboration: CBS ("multiple sources"); CNN (multiple current US officials briefed, 11/19 and 11/20); The Record (a source said Clayton's PHP remarks "were correct"); WSJ (one person familiar: the NSA "was simply updating its software to patch the system"); Nextgov (four of six people said the outage "may be linked to a series of software upgrades on the network").
- The NYT reported that the issue "appeared to be caused by a need to patch software with a system update," per one person. This is excerpt-only; the NYT page could not be scraped.
- Restoration also required patches. A senior administration official said the patching was "slower than expected" (CNN, 11/19) and "took longer than anticipated" (CNN, 11/20).
- The NSA itself has said only "scheduled routine maintenance" and gave no details of the cause (AP, Politico).
- A former senior NSA cybersecurity official with no direct knowledge speculated to The Guardian that several patches may have been applied at once.
core.trigger_change_date:
No source reports the date the NSA applied the patch to NSANet. Related dates:
- PHP released the fixed versions (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35) on 2026-10-21.
- NSA and CISA issued advisories urging immediate patching on 2026-10-21.
- CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26, with a federal deadline of 2026-10-29.
- On 2026-11-17 Clayton referred to "about 10 days ago" (CBS only).
- NYT (one person) and The Record (one source) said NSANet had been "unstable for weeks" before 11/17.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link:
YES, multiple sources tie the change to remediation of a security vulnerability.
- DNI Clayton directly linked the outage to patching that followed the PHP vulnerability disclosure (Fox Business, 11/17). The Record: "the outage was caused by a software patch intended to fix critical vulnerabilities discovered last month."
- CBS: the outage was "linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP," per multiple sources.
- CNN (11/19 and 11/20): multiple current US officials said it "appeared connected to the NSA's handling of software updates for vulnerabilities in PHP."
- Washington Sun (single outlet, three sources): the NSA told members of Congress the outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by AI.

The AI-found angle is reported inconsistently:
- CNN, CBS and NY Post say AI tools helped discover or exploit the flaws. CNN (10/21) names OpenAI, Wiz and Calif as the researchers; Wiz used Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and GPT-5.6 Sol.
- The PHP Foundation (10/21) says a PHP core developer found the first signs of the out-of-memory (OOM) root cause in 2024, while fixing an issue from a Quarkslab audit. Calif reported the RCE on 2026-08-11 during OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" audit; OpenAI and Wiz independently reported the same root cause or further attack vectors. PHP had been scanned earlier with Anthropic's Claude Mythos via Alpha-Omega, and OpenAI's Daybreak Red was used to validate reports.
- Federal News Network (10/27): "While humans first identified the vulnerabilities."
- The Record (11/18): "It remains unknown if the vulnerability was AI-derived or human-driven."

No denial of the PHP link was found. The NSA has neither confirmed nor denied it; its only statement cites "scheduled routine maintenance."
core.ai_statements:
The NSA itself made no AI-related statement about the incident (none found). Others did:
- Clayton, who chairs the White House Super Intelligence Force, told Fox Business that AI can scan systems "more quickly," so "the ability to identify vulnerabilities has increased," and "That is why it is so incumbent upon all of us to work together, to patch, to report vulnerabilities" (via GMA/ABC). He also said: "We need to continue with every iteration of these frontier models, engagement with the government, engagement with industry, to make sure that before the model is rolled out, we are dealing with the cyber issues" (Fox Business, 11/17).
- At the 11/18 House hearing Clayton said "the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago in a year are a lot older" (GMA).
- CNN (11/18) described the outage's repercussions as stemming from "what Trump administration officials on Wednesday described as a consequence of the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence."
- Sen. Mark Warner, Senate Intelligence vice chair, said in a 11/17 statement: "AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change... the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity" (AP, CNN).
- Washington Sun (single outlet): the NSA privately told Congress the outages stemmed from fixing vulnerabilities identified by AI models.
- A former military cyber operator told CNN that AI "also introduces new and hard-to-predict bugs." This is commentary, not an official statement.
core.cyberattack_statements:
Officials and sources consistently said there was no evidence of a cyberattack:
- CNN (six sources): "At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack."
- The Record: initially "not believed to be the result of a cyberattack," per two people familiar.
- Clayton (Fox Business, 11/17): "We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyber attack. And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here."
- Clayton (House Homeland Security, 11/18): the outages "are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." He cited a "very high level of confidence" and added, "They are different causes... Do we see any of them here? We do not see them."
- DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin: "We're 98% confident that there is no nefarious activity going on."
- Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio: "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors..."
- Senior administration official (background call, 11/18): "We have no indication that this is a cyberattack..."
- CNN (11/19, 11/20): multiple current US officials said "it was not a cyberattack."
- Two US officials told CBS there were no indications of a cyberattack. The WSJ's source said there was no evidence of one.

Dissent and scrutiny:
- Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a "dedicated red team" to "challenge the assumption that these outages are just business as usual," reporting to Congress by December 1 (The Record).
- Former DoD analyst Mike Wiacek questioned "how quickly officials ruled out an attack" (Guardian).

core.timing_notes:
All times are US Eastern Standard Time (UTC-5).

**Tue 11/17**
- Morning: outage under way. Day-shift "code yellow"; non-emergency staff told not to come in before noon (NYT via Guardian); staggered arrivals.
- 10:31 AM (15:31 UTC): CNN first report.
- Afternoon: NSA statement. Clayton tied the outage to PHP patching on Fox Business; the article was created 4:13 PM (21:13 UTC).
- Evening: the employee inbox reverted to "code green."
- Later Tuesday night: "code orange," closing the campus to most employees (CNN, Nextgov).
- Late Tuesday night: "Code Gray" set staggered arrival at 10 a.m. Wednesday, later pushed to the afternoon (The Record, Nextgov).

**Wed 11/18**
- CBS (two sources): "NSA Net as of right now is back up and running," but staggered arrival ("Code Gray") continued.
- The Record (one source): the network was working, but logins were staggered. The source guessed another day or two for full restoration.

**Thu 11/19**
- The voicemail moved to "code orange" again, extending the campus closure (CNN).
- A senior administration official said the patching was going "slower than expected."
- On several occasions, employees who reported on a staggered basis were sent home without logging in (CNN).

**Fri 11/20**
- CNN reported the outage resolved at 9:01 AM (14:01 UTC). Most staff were expected back by midday.

**Duration**
- Sources describe the duration as "more than three days" and "almost four days" (CNN), "nearly four days" (NY Post), and "three days" (TNND). No exact start or end timestamps were published, so duration_hours is left empty.

**Possible earlier instability**
- NYT (one person) and The Record (another person) said NSANet had been unstable for weeks before 11/17.
other_notable: NSA's statement does not name NSANet or give a cause. AP: the agency 'did not provide any additional details on the cause of the outage or the scope of the disruption.' Politico: 'The NSA did not provide details on which of its systems were impacted.'
Politico: it is unclear whether U.S. Cyber Command, which shares the Fort Meade campus and is led by the same commander, Gen. Joshua Rudd, was affected; Cyber Command did not respond.

CNN (four sources, single outlet): the outage affected the NSA cryptologic center in Georgia that oversees Middle East cyber operations amid the US war with Iran. Staff there used workarounds and backup systems.

One source told CNN that many old, heavily 'compartmented' NSA networks 'went untouched.' A former senior NSA official said NSANet 'wasn't designed, it evolved,' and that past NSANet outages during upgrades did not make the news.
Washington Sun (single outlet, three sources, 11/17): Wall Street executives and the NSA told members of Congress that the week's outages were caused by attempts to fix AI-identified vulnerabilities.

The incident came amid a cluster of US outages: the Microsoft Outlook/Teams outage (months-old bug), the FAA nationwide ground stop on 11/13-14 (router/telecom upgrade), JPMorgan Chase and other banks on 11/16, United Airlines, and Apple services on 11/17 (internal update). Officials said they were separate.
Schumer, on 11/18, called for an intelligence 'red team' to report to Congress by December 1. Jeffries called for briefings.

President Trump, traveling in Asia, said of the outages: 'Things like that happen... It's fine.' A current and a former US official said NSANet's outage would not affect delivery of urgent intelligence to the president (CNN).
Precedent: in 2000, an NSA computer failure downed systems for nearly three days (CNN, The Record).

core.trigger_change_description: Apple attributed the outage to an unspecified "internal update" and said it "caused some outages this morning" (Nov 17). Apple has not said what the update changed, which systems it targeted, or when it was first deployed. MacRumors calls it an "unspecified 'internal update'". eBuilder Security (Nov 18) wrote that Apple "has given no technical account of the update", has given no count of affected users or countries, and has promised no post-incident report. Nacionale's Nov 18 roundup lists "What Apple's internal update changed, and why it hit so many services at once" under what is not known. A few outlets, such as a CBS LA video caption and an Indian outlet, describe it as an "internal software update". That wording comes from those outlets, not from Apple's statement.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link: No source ties Apple's internal update to a security fix, vulnerability remediation, or a flaw found by AI. Apple did not describe what the update was for. Its only stated denial is that the outage was not caused by a cyberattack. No source reports Apple either confirming or denying a security purpose. Several officials made general statements about the week's outages as a group, but none named Apple's update as a security patch: (1) DNI Jay Clayton, on Fox Business, said the incidents came from security upgrades, such as plugging the PHP flaws, that took longer than planned or hit unexpected problems (Guardian, Nov 18). At the House Homeland Security hearing on Nov 18 he called them "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes" (CBS). (2) Sen. Mark Warner: "The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity" (Guardian). He also said AI is creating pressure to patch vulnerabilities immediately (AFR/Bloomberg). (3) Secretary of State Rubio, asked about the role of AI: "sometimes, when you are going in to fix the system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption... I would refer you to the company" (White House pool report). The Next Web juxtaposes Clayton's patching explanation with Apple's outage, but it does not say Apple's update was a patch.
core.ai_statements: No statement from Apple mentioning AI in connection with the outage was found. Official statements about AI concerned the wave of outages in general, not Apple specifically: (1) Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Nov 17 in Manila (White House pool report, Nov 18): "sometimes, when you are going in to fix the system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption in the way the system works. That's how that's how it's been described to me in terms of the role that that that SI. might have played in it. I don't want to speculate on it because again, every one of these instances is distinct and unique, and I would refer you to the company." https://www.forth.news/whpool/Ch9ZeExjba4mguZHMTm4F (2) Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Fox News that artificial intelligence ("super-intelligence", or "SI") could be behind the recent outages (Guardian, Nov 17). https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/17/gmail-apple-outage-major-disruption (3) Sen. Mark Warner said the outages appear to be the "consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape" (AFR/Bloomberg). https://www.afr.com/world/north-america/apple-update-sparks-outage-at-internal-retail-and-icloud-operations-20261118-p61f46
core.cyberattack_statements: Apple said the outage was not caused by a cyberattack (Reuters, Bloomberg via MacRumors and AFR, TIME, CBS, AppleInsider). Government statements about the outage wave in general: Rubio said "zero evidence" that the outages are linked or are the work of malign actors (Guardian, Nov 18; White House pool report). At the House Homeland Security hearing on Nov 18 (CBS): DHS Secretary Mullin said "We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related" and that he was "98% confident" they were not malicious foreign activity; DNI Clayton said "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack"; FBI Deputy Director Raia said "there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents."

core.what_failed: AWS reported signup errors, authentication issues and connectivity issues in US-EAST-1. (1) IAM Identity Center sign-in requests and AWS Sign Up failed. Customers who used IAM Identity Center to sign in to the AWS Console, or to services that depend on it such as Kiro and Amazon Connect, got errors. AWS said "There are no workarounds for impacted customers." Kiro logins through social sign-in were not affected. AWS fully mitigated the authentication problem at 5:20 AM PST. (2) A subset of Network Load Balancers in a single cell of a single Availability Zone (use1-az1) kept having connectivity issues until AWS "fully mitigated the underlying issue" at 6:21 AM PST. AWS listed 11 impacted services: AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS IoT Device Management, AWS NAT Gateway, AWS Sign Up, AWS Step Functions, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Connect, Amazon Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon VPC Lattice and Kiro. AWS has not published a technical root cause, and none of its updates say whether the authentication failure and the NLB failure share a cause. (Sources: AWS Health Dashboard event page; Control Plane, Nov 18; GBHackers, Nov 16.)

core.vulnerability_remediation_link: Not mentioned for this incident. No source found ties the Nov 15 AWS outage to a security fix, vulnerability remediation or AI-found flaw, and no AWS statement either confirming or denying such a link was found. Context: (a) A cluster-wide narrative held that the Nov 12-17 US outages came from rushed patches for AI-found vulnerabilities. It traces to The Washington Sun (anonymous sources), Sen. Mark Warner's statements and DNI remarks, as reported by the FT on Nov 18, Fortune on Nov 18 and MLQ. None of the coverage reviewed names AWS among the outages attributed to patching: the FT lists Microsoft, JPMorgan, the FAA and the NSA, and Fortune names the NSA and the banks. (b) The Cloud Security Alliance note of Nov 18 lists AWS's cause as "Not disclosed" and cyberattack ruled out as "Not addressed". It omits AWS from its attribution table "because it made no public statement on malicious causation", and it says the claim that AI-found-vulnerability patching caused any specific outage in the cluster "is unsupported." (c) RCR Wireless (Nov 19) says AWS reported its trouble "without a public root-cause explanation sufficient to connect it to the others." (d) Separately, in the weeks before the outage AWS was patching its infrastructure for CVE-2026-98432, a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP flaw. That work included the infrastructure under TLS listeners on Network Load Balancer, plus network-level protections; see recent_security_patch_activity. No source connects that work to the Nov 15 NLB or Identity Center failures.
core.ai_statements: No official AWS or Amazon statement mentioning AI in connection with this incident was found, including no denial. Kiro, AWS's AI coding tool, appears in AWS's updates only as an affected service. Unrelated context: in February 2026 Amazon published "Correcting the Financial Times report about AWS, Kiro, and AI," saying a different (December 2025) interruption "was the result of user error—specifically misconfigured access controls—not AI" (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-service-outage-ai-bot-kiro). That statement concerns a different incident.
core.cyberattack_statements: AWS's Health Dashboard and AWS Support updates do not mention a cyberattack or malicious activity; Control Plane, Cybersecurity News, GBHackers and SecurTek all say so. core.what_failed: Nov 16 (keyed event): the switches (交換機) that carry Docomo's 5G SA subscribers. Docomo said traffic concentrated on them ("交換機への通信の集中"). Voice, data and SMS were hard to use nationwide for 5G SA subscribers only, and phones could show "out of service". MVNOs on Docomo's network, emergency calls, and non-SA 5G and 4G users were not affected. Partial recovery: about 60% of affected customers by the 13:30-14:30 JST reports, 95% or more at 15:30, full recovery at 15:58 JST (Docomo reports 5-7 and the restoration notice). Docomo's first notice said the problem might affect all Docomo lines and MVNOs, with the start time "確認中" (being checked); later notices narrowed it to 5G SA. Nov 11: "congestion" (輻輳) of the same switches, 10:34-19:17 JST (8h43m). Nov 5-6: congestion of the same switches, about 11:18 Nov 5 to about 01:20 Nov 6 JST (about 14h), up to about 1.587 million lines. At a Nov 6 briefing Docomo said the Nov 5 event began during core-network maintenance work. A memory anomaly appeared in part of the switch (the call-control part). A defect in its counterpart device ("カウンター装置") caused repeated searches for a connection destination. Registration processing slowed, devices sent many retransmission requests, and the central device became congested. The memory anomaly was in the active (現用系) unit. Diagnosis was slowed by a nationwide subscriber-database file update running in parallel at the same time.

core.trigger_change_description: Nov 16 (keyed event): no source names a triggering change, maintenance work or software update. Docomo gave the cause only as concentration of traffic on the 5G SA switches, and listed it as "調査中" (under investigation) until the 15:58 restoration notice. Nov 11: no trigger named either; the cause was given only as switch congestion. Asahi reports Docomo said the Nov 5 and Nov 11 causes "differ", and Kyodo reports Docomo said the mechanism differed between the first and second outages. Nov 5: Docomo said at its Nov 6 briefing that the outage began during core-network maintenance work (保守作業), when a memory anomaly occurred in the call-control part of a 5G SA switch. A nationwide subscriber-database file update was running in parallel in the same time window. Docomo said the work procedure itself had no problem and blamed a defect in a counterpart device. Remediation: Docomo said a provisional measure to prevent the memory anomaly was already done, and a permanent measure would be finished within one week of Nov 6, along with tighter construction governance, such as not running related works at the same time. Mobilelaby (single source) reports that Docomo PR said after the Nov 16 outage that this permanent measure was still not complete, and could not say whether it would prevent outages like the second and third.
core.trigger_change_date: 2026-11-05 (the maintenance work and subscriber-DB file update that coincided with the Nov 5 outage; sources give no start time). No triggering change has been identified for the Nov 11 or Nov 16 outages.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link: Not mentioned. No source ties any of the three 5G SA outages, the Nov 5 core-network maintenance work, or the parallel subscriber-database file update to a security fix, a vulnerability remediation, or an AI-found flaw. Docomo's notices for all three outages say its investigation found no sign of unauthorized access or cyberattack before or after the event. Separately and at the same time, Docomo was responding to an unrelated breach: unauthorized access to its Docomo Online Shop and My docomo was detected around 10:30 JST on Nov 4, both services went into emergency maintenance from about 01:05 JST on Nov 5, and Docomo modified the My docomo, Online Shop and ahamo sign-up systems. No source links that remediation to the core-network work. Secondary outlet shattered.io states the sources do not tie the breach to either outage.
core.ai_statements: No official Docomo or government statement mentioning AI in connection with the three outages was found, including denials. Context, not linked to the cause: (1) Toyo Keizai (Nov 9) reports a question at the Nov 6 briefing on whether the 5G core's full virtualization and auto-recovery (April 2026) and the recovery AI agent Docomo presented in June had worked. Tsuboya said virtualization was "機能としては十分に生きている". Toyo Keizai says no detailed explanation was given of how AI agents were used in this outage. (2) Toyo Keizai reports that at a June 8, 2026 press tour of its network operations center, Docomo said it had used AI in earnest since FY2025 Q4: five purpose-specific AIs that cut initial fault-response time by 60%, including one that judges whether an ongoing fault comes from planned work, and an AI agent that cut recovery time for complex faults by 50% or more. (3) A March 2, 2026 NEC/Docomo press release says Docomo's commercial 5G core on AWS (launched Feb 26, 2026) was built using agentic-AI-automated design and construction. No source connects this to the outages.

core.timing_notes: Durations: Nov 16 10:02-15:58 JST = 01:02-06:58 UTC, 5h56m (Docomo; matches the MIC minister's "約5時間56分"). Nov 11 10:34-19:17 JST = 01:34-10:17 UTC, 8h43m. Nov 5 about 11:18 JST to Nov 6 about 01:20 JST = Nov 5 02:18-16:20 UTC, about 14h. All three started on weekday mornings (Yahoo News pickup note). Discrepancies in secondary sources: DCD calls the first outage "a 14-hour outage on November 6" and "last Friday", but Nov 5, 2026 was a Thursday. Asahi gives Nov 11 recovery as about 19:15 versus Docomo's 19:17. Selectra gives Nov 11 as about 8h45m. Asahi gives Nov 16 as about 10:00 to 16:00. Nov 16 sequence: the first notice said all Docomo lines and MVNOs might be affected, with the start time "確認中". It was later narrowed to 5G SA only. The cause stayed "調査中" until the 15:58 restoration notice. Earlier 5G SA-only nationwide outages: Aug 15, 2023 and Apr 3, 2024, each restored in about an hour (Toyo Keizai). Docomo announced full virtualization of its mobile core, with auto-healing, on Apr 2, 2026. On Nov 4, the day before the first outage, its earnings briefing raised FY capex by 43 billion yen to 900 billion yen, with more spending on 5G SA network equipment. MIC (Nov 17) asked Docomo for root-cause analysis of how the outages relate and for structural risk-management issues, and said it would act under relevant laws. The minister gave no deadline.
other_notable: Same-week security incident: Docomo disclosed on Nov 5 an unauthorized-access breach of Docomo Online Shop and My docomo, up to 294,839 lines (204,157 individual contracts), and is considering compensation payments. It is officially separate from the outages (ITmedia, Docomo notices).
Oct 16, 2026: an emergency earthquake alert sent by other carriers did not reach Docomo users via emergency SMS (Toyo Keizai).
Docomo said the permanent fix for the Nov 5 memory anomaly would be done within a week of Nov 6. Mobilelaby (single source) reports Docomo PR said it was still not complete after Nov 16.
Asahi (Nov 11, Nov 16) reports Docomo was investigating whether the outages are related.
Maeda said a 30 billion yen network-investment reduction plan toward FY2027 was not related to the outage (K-tai Watch).
Customer guidance during the outages was to switch to 4G and restart or toggle airplane mode; after recovery, Docomo asked customers to switch back.
Selectra notes that none of the outages reached the 24-hour threshold for compensation in Docomo's 5G service terms.

Telcel first described it to media as a "degradación en algunas localidades de Región 9" with "intermitencia en el servicio". Its later official statement said a "falla" happened during capacity-increase work on its network. Telcel said the origin was resolved immediately, but congestion from call attempts meant affected users would get service back gradually. La Jornada reported that Telcel and Telmex users in Mexico City and the metro area had no calls or mobile internet for about five hours. Telmex fixed and Wi-Fi complaints and AT&T, Movistar and Totalplay complaints were also logged the same day. No source has confirmed a common cause across carriers.

core.trigger_change_description: Telcel's official statement names "trabajos de incremento de capacidad en nuestra red" (capacity-increase work on its network) as the origin of the failure. Milenio paraphrases it as "trabajos de mejora e incremento de capacidad en su red", and La Jornada's headline calls it "trabajos de ampliación". Telcel did not say what kind of work it was (hardware, software or configuration), which network element was involved, whether the work was scheduled, or when it started. Infobae: "La empresa no fijó un horario de restablecimiento completo ni detalló el tipo específico de trabajos de red que originaron la falla." Telcel also named a secondary factor: congestion from call attempts slowed recovery. No source gives the date or time the capacity work was originally carried out or started.
core.vulnerability_remediation_link: Not mentioned. No source found ties the capacity-increase work to a security fix, vulnerability remediation or an AI-found flaw, and no denial on this point was found either. Before Telcel's statement, El Imparcial wrote (media, not official): "Por ahora, tampoco existe evidencia confirmada de que la interrupción esté relacionada con un ciberataque o hackeo."
core.ai_statements: No official statement mentioning AI was found from Telcel, América Móvil, Grupo Carso, AT&T México or the CRT regulator. The only AI references found are media labels for AI-generated illustrations or text (for example, Milenio image captions "IA M2" / "IA Discover"). These are not statements about the incident.
core.cyberattack_statements: No official statement on a cyberattack, either claiming or denying one, was found from Telcel or the authorities. Media: El Imparcial (before Telcel's explanation) said there was no confirmed evidence of a cyberattack or hack and that any explanation would be speculative (https://www.elimparcial.com/mexico/2026/11/20/telcel-registra-fallas-en-mexico-y-usuarios-reportan-problemas-con-llamadas-internet-y-senal-este-20-de-noviembre/). El Debate reported social-media rumors of a 72-hour global "apagón tecnológico", which it said specialists had dismissed, and stated the Telcel failure was not related to such an event (https://www.debate.com.mx/tecnologia/que-pasa-con-la-senal-de-telcel-esto-se-sabe-sobre-la-falla-nacional-y-los-rumores-de-apagon-20261120-0120.html). Telcel's official explanation was capacity-increase work, not an attack.

core.recent_security_patch_activity: No security patching, emergency patching or security maintenance by Telcel/América Móvil (or any named system vendor) was found for the 30 days before November 20, 2026. Searches found no announced maintenance window for November 2026. The only Telcel vulnerability coverage found is from January 2026: a flaw in the mandatory line-registration portal, which Telcel called a technical error it corrected immediately (https://expansion.mx/empresas/2026/01/12/telcel-niega-filtracion-masiva-de-datos). That is outside the 30-day window.
core.scale: Telcel says the affected area was "algunas localidades de la Ciudad de México y el área conurbada" (official statement), which it also called Región 9: CDMX metro area, Estado de México, Hidalgo and Morelos (Milenio, Infobae citing El Financiero). Downdetector counts: just under 1,000 complaints in 15 minutes near 11:00, and 3,708 by about 12:13, against a usual average of about 15 (Expansión, Infobae, El Debate). SinEmbargo alone reports a peak of 4,295 Telcel reports at 13:00 (single source). Reports also came from Guadalajara, Saltillo, Toluca, Ecatepec, Puebla, Oaxaca, Veracruz, Querétaro and other places. The same day, AT&T México peaked at 138 reports (13:11), Telmex at 128 and Totalplay at 128 (13:57), all per SinEmbargo (single source). Telcel had 81.78 million lines at the end of Q3 (Milenio). Infobae cites IFT Q2 2026 data putting Telcel at about 59% of active mobile lines. No official count of affected users was published.
core.timing_notes: Times are CST (UTC-6). Timeline: about 11:00, user reports start climbing on Downdetector. 12:13, 3,708 Downdetector reports. Around 12:16 to 12:49, Telcel answers individual users on X asking for direct messages but gives no explanation. 13:30, La Jornada publishes the Grupo Carso "degradación... región 9" quote. 14:24, Excélsior publishes the spokesperson quote, which it says came "casi dos horas después de la caída". About 14:00, AT&T México posts on X that its network is operating normally; N+ reports that some areas had regained signal while others still had problems. 17:25 (23:25:27 UTC), Telcel posts its official communiqué on X (post ID 2123920688796864869; the timestamp comes from the X post metadata and the El Financiero embed "11:25 p. m. · 20 nov. 2026"). Media coverage of it followed: Quadratín at 18:44 and El Universal at 19:14. Duration: La Jornada says "unas cinco horas" and Milenio says "al menos 5 horas". El Universal reports users saying at least three hours. Telcel gave no full-restoration time, so no official end time exists and end_utc is left blank. Five hours from an 11:00 start would put the end around 16:00 CST / 22:00 UTC, but no source states that. Reuters says the outage came just over a month after mid-October outages.
other_notable: AT&T México denied any fault in its network and attributed its customers' difficulties reaching other carriers to 'causas ajenas a nuestra red' (La Jornada; Reuters).
Reuters reported outages affecting Telcel, AT&T Mexico and Movistar. Spokespeople for América Móvil and Movistar, and the regulator CRT, did not immediately respond to Reuters.
La Jornada reported that Telmex (fixed) users also complained of interruptions. Downdetector Telmex complaints were mainly Wi-Fi (51%) and broadband (35%) (SinEmbargo).
Telcel did not detail any compensation in its statement (Primera Línea). N+ published an explainer on legal bonification rules (not less than 20% of the price paid).

Earlier 2026 Telcel outages with no official cause found: Aug 17 (Tiempo/Crónica), Oct 13 (El Imparcial), Oct 15 (Publimetro), and mid-October per Reuters. N+ described Nov 20 as the first Telcel failure in six months, which conflicts with those reports.
A Telcel 'technical vulnerability' in the line-registration portal was reported in January 2026 (outside the 30-day window).
No CRT, Profeco or other government statement specific to this outage was found as of the searches.

Downstream effects of one root event sit inside the root entry and are not counted separately: Workday on Feb 20 is inside Cloudflare, and Coinbase and Heroku on May 7-8 are inside AWS. own_change_incidents covers the categories 'own change: update/patch/deploy/config' and 'own change: maintenance/hardware work'.
